paper_title: SFT WITHOUT OVERFITTING: ANALYZING THE TRAINING DYNAMICS OF SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
paper_description: Selective fine-tuning of Transformer modules (attention vs. feedforward) to preserve OOD generalization on GeneralPoints (arithmetic) and V-IRL (navigation) benchmarks. Claims attention-only SFT preserves OOD performance while full/FNN-only SFT causes memorization collapse.

weaknesses.pattern: Only 2 rule-based reasoning benchmarks → Impossible to claim findings apply broadly to SFT dynamics

reviewer_quote.text: if the method needs tuning for each specific task that definitely takes quite a bit away from its appeal. Transformers are amazing (in part) because they require little tuning from task to task.

weaknesses.why_applies: GeneralPoints and V-IRL are both narrow, structured tasks. Different reasoning types (language understanding, commonsense, symbolic manipulation) may show completely different patterns. Reviewers will question generalizability.
required_fixes: Add 3-5 additional benchmarks spanning diverse reasoning types
Show consistent selective attention advantage across different task types
Analyze task characteristics that influence which modules should be tuned

weaknesses.pattern: No clear explanation of WHY selective attention tuning works for OOD → Results appear empirical accident

reviewer_quote.text: The foundational hypothesis that 'PLMs encapsulate multiple pieces of knowledge as subnetworks' lacks supporting references or verification experiments. Although empirical results support DST's effectiveness, the Introduction lacks a clear causal rationale for these core design choices.

weaknesses.why_applies: Paper likely shows that attention-only SFT preserves OOD performance, but without mechanistic insight into WHY, reviewers view it as task-specific luck. Why does attention help? Is it attention modularity? Lower memorization capacity? Different gradient flow?
required_fixes: Provide mechanistic explanation via gradient analysis or representation study
Analyze what happens to attention weights/patterns during SFT vs. FNN weights
Measure effective memorization capacity of each module type
Show gradient flow differences between attention and FNN

weaknesses.category: Memorization vs. Generalization Not Clearly Distinguished
weaknesses.pattern: Claimed 'OOD generalization improvements' may actually be just 'regularization from smaller effective capacity'

reviewer_quote.text: Most evaluations, including the ablation studies, focus on downstream tasks, which are interesting and practically relevant but do not provide clear insight into what the algorithm is doing at the shift-invariance level. They also add confounding factors.

weaknesses.why_applies: Must separately measure: (1) ID accuracy (training rules), (2) OOD accuracy (held-out rules), (3) the gap between them. Without this, improvements could just reflect that attention-only tunes fewer parameters (regularization), not true generalization.
required_fixes: Report ID and OOD performance separately for all methods
Show that attention-only maintains in-distribution accuracy while improving OOD
If ID accuracy drops with attention-only, acknowledge as trade-off not a win
Analyze the ID-OOD gap directly as the generalization measure

weaknesses.pattern: Unclear how to choose which modules to fine-tune on new tasks → Method requires per-task tuning

reviewer_quote.text: The algorithm may rely on selecting hyperparameters (e.g. s and q) for removing the slowest and fastest examples. And it might be unclear how that parameter varies across different datasets. If choosing hyperparameters via repetitive experiments, then it may defeat the premise of continual learning.

weaknesses.why_applies: If selective module selection must be tuned for each task, the method isn't practical. Reviewers will ask: How do I know whether to use attention-only for a new task? What if different tasks need different modules?
required_fixes: Develop clear criteria for module selection that transfer to new domains
Test module selection strategy on completely new benchmark
Or show that same module selection (e.g., 'always attention-only') works across diverse tasks
Provide guidance for practitioners on how to choose modules for new domains

weaknesses.pattern: Only 3 methods (full FT, FNN-only, attention-only) compared on 2 benchmarks → Insufficient evidence for causal claims

reviewer_quote.text: L_KDL is not ablated to show its usefulness in this work. Some code or pseudocode would strengthen knowing how the KSL/KDM is actually implemented.

weaknesses.why_applies: Missing ablations: selective percentages (25%/50%/75% of attention layers), different base models, interaction with model size. Missing baselines: LoRA, BitFit, adapters, full FT + L2 regularization, full FT + early stopping on OOD validation.
required_fixes: Ablation on selective percentages: 50% vs 75% vs 90% of attention layers
Compare against LoRA, BitFit, adapter-based fine-tuning, other parameter-efficient methods
Test full fine-tuning with explicit regularization (L2, dropout) as baseline
Test on 2-3 different model sizes to show interaction effects
Ablation on which layers matter most (early vs late attention layers?)

weaknesses.pattern: Unknown if findings hold for large, modern language models and diverse architectures

reviewer_quote.text: Llama 2-7B is relatively old, experiments on 3/3.1/3.2 would be better.

weaknesses.why_applies: Attention/FNN specialization may be specific to model size/architecture tested. Modern large models may have different module properties. Different attention mechanisms (GQA, MQA) or instruction-tuning may change results.
required_fixes: Test on at least 2 different model scales (e.g., 7B and 13B)
Show pattern consistency across model scales
Consider testing on different base model families if applicable
Explicitly discuss scalability limitations

weaknesses.pattern: No theory explaining why selective attention tuning improves OOD generalization

reviewer_quote.text: No explanation or intuition is provided as to why medium learning speed items are the most useful for populating memory. It would be good if the authors provided a rationale beyond the empirical results.

weaknesses.why_applies: Without theory or detailed intuition, the contribution feels shallow: 'We tried this and it worked, but don't know why.' Reviewers expect either theoretical analysis or detailed empirical analysis of the mechanism.
required_fixes: Provide theoretical intuition for why attention is more modular than FNNs
Analyze gradient flow differences between module types
Show empirical evidence of representation changes in each module
Compare attention vs FNN specialization across different reasoning types

weaknesses.pattern: OOD settings unclear; no statistical significance testing with confidence intervals

reviewer_quote.text: Some of the results indicate improvement when averaged over multiple runs. But in some of those cases based on the standard deviations computed there is a fair overlap between prior methods and your method, it's possible that the advantage in those cases is not so clear when there is a large variance.

weaknesses.why_applies: Need: (1) Clear definition of OOD for both benchmarks, (2) Multiple seeds (5-10) with statistical significance tests, (3) Confidence intervals not just mean±SD, (4) Analysis of which OOD settings are hardest.
required_fixes: Explicitly define OOD distributions: what exactly changes in held-out evaluation?
Report results over 5-10 random seeds
Use confidence intervals and statistical significance tests (t-test, Mann-Whitney U)
Analyze difficulty of different OOD settings
Compare OOD gaps across methods statistically

weaknesses.pattern: No investigation of when selective SFT fails or underperforms baselines

reviewer_quote.text: Although the authors show that the results achieved are better than other alternatives, the benefit is only marginal. Often even less than the standard deviation. During the analysis, the difference is often at most 2%, between all removal combinations.

weaknesses.why_applies: Paper likely shows average performance improvements. But without error analysis or per-instance analysis, reviewers won't know: when does attention-only fail? which reasoning types benefit most? Are improvements within noise?
required_fixes: Identify failure cases: when does attention-only underperform full FT?
Analyze per-reasoning-type performance (which rule types benefit most?)
Provide per-example error analysis or visualization
Report improvements with confidence intervals and significance tests

weaknesses.pattern: No analysis of computational cost, training time, inference speed of selective SFT vs. full FT

reviewer_quote.text: Although the KSL is smaller compared to the size of the model, it must have some sort of slow-down associated with it. What is the speed reduction in using this method?

weaknesses.why_applies: 2% OOD improvement is useless if it costs 50% more training time or memory. Must measure: training time, memory usage, inference latency, hyperparameter selection cost.
required_fixes: Report wall-clock training time for all methods
Analyze memory usage during training (peak memory, total memory)
Report inference latency if different from standard FT
Quantify cost of determining which modules to tune
Discuss training-inference trade-offs clearly

weaknesses.pattern: GeneralPoints and V-IRL may have specific properties that favor selective attention tuning

reviewer_quote.text: The paper only explores ResNet and its smaller variants... For other architectures such as transformers, VGG net, etc do the same conclusions stand?

weaknesses.why_applies: Both benchmarks are structured, rule-based. Other reasoning types (language understanding, commonsense) might show different patterns. Could simpler methods (standard FT + regularization) achieve same results?
required_fixes: Analyze task characteristics: why might these favor attention-only?
Add diverse reasoning benchmarks beyond rule-based tasks
Compare to baseline: standard FT + L2 regularization
Show selective attention is genuinely better, not just a regularization effect

tier1_must_dos: Expand benchmarks to 3+ diverse reasoning tasks
Provide mechanistic explanation for selective attention advantage
Add missing baselines: LoRA, BitFit, efficient FT methods
Test on 2+ model scales for scalability evidence
tier2_should_dos: Comprehensive ablations on selective percentages and layers
Statistical significance testing (5-10 seeds, confidence intervals)
Computational cost analysis (training time, memory, inference)
Error analysis: failure modes and hard reasoning types
Clear hyperparameter selection guidance for new domains
tier3_nice_to_haves: Visualization of learning dynamics across modules
Task characteristic analysis explaining benchmark properties
Comparison with other selective fine-tuning methods

sources.analysis_methodology: Extracted common reviewer weakness patterns from ICLR 2025 human reviews of related papers (fine-tuning, memorization, OOD generalization, parameter-efficient methods) and applied to SFT paper with specific quotes and actionable fixes
